title: Činggis qan-i …
about: Around 1225, as the Mongol army came home from its conquest of Central Asia, Chinggis Qan gathered his lords, and his nephew Yisüngge made an arrow-shot so long that it was cut in stone: 335 alds, about half a kilometre. These five lines are the oldest surviving text in the Mongol script, the alphabet the Mongols took over from the Uyghurs, written in columns from top to bottom with the columns following one another from left to right, as it is still written in Inner Mongolia today. The carver raised the first line and the fourth above the rest, so that the names of Chinggis and of Yisüngge stand higher than everything else on the stone. Some things to know as you read. The script writes several sounds with one shape (o and u, ö and ü, t and d, q and γ before some vowels), so the romanized line beside each column carries the reading the script leaves open. The text is set here in a modern Mongol typeface, which smooths the cut letters into their present-day shapes; the photographs show the stone itself, and a cast of it in Hohhot on which the letters are easier to see. The stone has been read for two centuries and the reading is settled almost everywhere, but a crack has destroyed the first letter of the place-name in line 3, and the archery word ontudur is still discussed. The notes say where.
source: The Stele of Yisüngge, the 'Chinggis Stone' (c. 1224–1225), found in 1802 near the ruins of Khirkhira in Transbaikalia, in the Hermitage Museum, St Petersburg, since 1936. The text is the inscription itself, which no one owns; the reading follows the standard decipherment as stated by I. de Rachewiltz (East Asian History 42, 2010), consulted for readings only, with the line layout checked against photographs of the stone and of its cast in the Inner Mongolia Museum. The five lines are kept as the stone's five columns; its raising of lines 1 and 4 is described but not reproduced. Encoding: Unicode Mongolian, with suffixes written apart from their words where the reading hyphenates them. Romanization: the conventional scholarly romanization of written Mongolian (q γ č ǰ š ö ü; suffixes hyphenated), the same convention as Lectorium's Classical Mongolian texts. The language is pre-classical Mongolian of Chinggis's own time, the stage that also gave the Secret History. Translations are made fresh from the Mongolian for this edition.

images.caption: The stone itself in the Hermitage, St Petersburg: a slab about two metres tall. The five lines run down the middle of its face, and the pale crack that crosses it took the first letter of the place-name in line 3.
images.alt: A tall, round-topped granite slab on a white plinth in a museum room, faint vertical lines of script down its face

sentences.t:
ᠴᠢᠩᠭᠢᠰ ᠬᠠᠨ ᠢ
ᠰᠠᠷᠲᠠᠭᠤᠯ ᠢᠷᠭᠡ ᠳᠠᠭᠤᠯᠢᠵᠤ ᠪᠠᠭᠤᠵᠤ ᠬᠠᠮᠤᠭ ᠮᠣᠩᠭᠣᠯ ᠤᠯᠤᠰ ᠤᠨ
ᠨᠣᠶᠠᠳ ᠢ ᠪᠤᠬᠠ ᠰᠣᠴᠢᠭᠠᠢ ᠬᠤᠷᠢᠭᠰᠠᠨ ᠳᠤᠷ
sentences.tr:
Činggis qan-i
Sartaγul irge daγuliǰu baγuǰu qamuγ Mongγol ulus-un
noyad-i Buqa Sočiγai quriγsan-dur
sentences.l: Chinggis Qan — the Sartaul people having-plundered, having-encamped — of the whole Mongol nation the lords at Buqa Sočiγai at-[his]-having-gathered,
sentences.i: When Chinggis Qan, having plundered the Sartaul people, had made camp and gathered the lords of the whole Mongol nation at Buqa Sočiγai,
sentences.n:
Lines 1–3 are a single long time-clause. Mongolian puts the verb last: everything here builds toward quriγsan-dur, 'at (his) having gathered', and only then does the main sentence begin. The two -ǰu forms (daγuliǰu, baγuǰu) chain actions: 'having plundered, having made camp'. You'll see this chaining constantly in Mongolian narrative.
Činggis qan-i carries the accusative -i, though Chinggis is the one doing the gathering. Middle Mongol can mark the subject of a participle clause this way; grammarians explain the usage in more than one way.
Line 1 holds only Chinggis's name and title, set higher on the stone than lines 2 and 3, out of respect.
Buqa Sočiγai stands bare, with no 'at' after it, as place-names often do. A crack runs through its first letter; the S is restored, supported by a Persian history (Rashīd al-Dīn) that gives the place as Buqa Sučïγu.

sentences.t:
ᠶᠢᠰᠦᠩᠭᠡ ᠣᠨᠲᠤᠳᠤᠷ ᠤᠨ ᠭᠤᠷᠪᠠᠨ ᠵᠠᠭᠤᠳ ᠭᠤᠴᠢᠨ ᠲᠠᠪᠤᠨ ᠠᠯᠳᠠᠰ
ᠲᠤᠷ ᠣᠨᠲᠤᠳᠤᠯᠠᠭ᠎ᠠ
sentences.tr:
Yisüngge ontudur-un γurban ǰaγud γučin tabun aldas-
tur ontudulaγ-a
sentences.l: Yisüngge — of the mark-shot, at three hundreds thirty five alds — shot-at-the-mark.
sentences.i: Yisüngge shot an arrow at a mark three hundred and thirty-five alds away.
sentences.n:
Line 4 begins with Yisüngge's name and is raised like line 1, so the stone honours the archer next to the Qan.
Numbers are built as in English: γurban ǰaγud γučin tabun, 'three hundreds thirty five'. 335 alds is roughly 530 metres, an enormous distance for an arrow, which is why it was carved in stone.
ontudur and ontudulaγ-a appear to share one root, usually linked with onu- 'to hit the mark', so the sentence says, in effect, that he 'mark-shot a mark-shot of 335 alds'. Scholars agree on the sense and differ on the exact letters: some read the verb ontudlaγa; the reading here, ontudulaγa, rests on a re-examination of the stone itself.
The suffix -tur ('at') was cut at the top of line 5 because line 4 ran out of room after aldas.

glossary.ᠴᠢᠩᠭᠢᠰ: Činggis — Chinggis, the title Temüjin took in 1206 when he was raised as ruler of all the Mongols (what the name means is debated)
glossary.ᠬᠠᠨ: qan — ruler, khan; the contracted form of qaγan, 'emperor'
glossary.ᠢ: -i — accusative case particle, written apart from its word. After Činggis qan it marks the man who does the gathering in the clause that follows (see note); after noyad it marks the lords who are gathered
glossary.ᠰᠠᠷᠲᠠᠭᠤᠯ: Sartaγul — the Sartauls: the Muslim town people of Central Asia; here the subjects of the Khwarazm-shah, whose empire the Mongols overran in 1219–1223
glossary.ᠢᠷᠭᠡ: irge — people, subjects (the later form is irgen)
glossary.ᠳᠠᠭᠤᠯᠢᠵᠤ: daγuliǰu — daγuli- 'to raid, plunder, make war on' + -ǰu, the converb 'having …', which chains one action to the next
glossary.ᠪᠠᠭᠤᠵᠤ: baγuǰu — baγu- 'to dismount, come down, make camp' + -ǰu 'having …' (converb)
glossary.ᠤᠯᠤᠰ: ulus — people, nation; the realm a ruler's people make up
glossary.ᠤᠨ: -un — genitive particle, 'of', written apart from its word (form used after a consonant)
glossary.ᠨᠣᠶᠠᠳ: noyad — lords, commanders; plural of noyan
glossary.ᠪᠤᠬᠠ: Buqa — 'bull'; the first half of the place-name Buqa Sočiγai
glossary.ᠰᠣᠴᠢᠭᠠᠢ: Sočiγai — the second half of the place-name, from soči- 'to start, take fright' (said of an animal); the whole name seems to mean 'where the bull takes fright'. Its first letter is lost in a crack in the stone
glossary.ᠬᠤᠷᠢᠭᠰᠠᠨ: quriγsan — quri- 'to gather, assemble' + -γsan, past participle: 'having gathered'
glossary.ᠳᠤᠷ: -dur — dative-locative particle, 'at, in'; on a participle it means 'at the time of', so quriγsan-dur is 'when (he) had gathered'
glossary.ᠶᠢᠰᠦᠩᠭᠡ: Yisüngge — usually identified as the son of Chinggis's brother Qasar, so the Qan's nephew; a famous archer
glossary.ᠣᠨᠲᠤᠳᠤᠷ: ontudur — a shot at a mark, a target-shot. The word is usually linked with onu- 'to hit the mark'; its exact form and sense are not certain (see note)
glossary.ᠵᠠᠭᠤᠳ: ǰaγud — hundreds; plural of ǰaγun 'hundred' (γurban ǰaγud = three hundred)
glossary.ᠠᠯᠳᠠᠰ: aldas — alds; plural of alda, the span of a man's outstretched arms, roughly 1.6 m
glossary.ᠲᠤᠷ: -tur — dative-locative particle, 'at' (the form used after s); it stands at the top of line 5 because the stone's line broke after aldas
glossary.ᠣᠨᠲᠤᠳᠤᠯᠠᠭᠠ: ontudulaγa — shot at the mark: a verb from the same root as ontudur, with the past-tense ending -laγa. The final -a is written as a separate stroke
